questions.stem: Several monoclonal antibodies are now used as anticancer drugs. Which of the following monoclonal antibody is implicated in causing cardiomyopathy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Trastuzumab

 

  • Trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody used primarily in the treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer, is associated with cardiotoxicity, including cardiomyopathy and heart failure. The mechanism of this cardiotoxicity is not fully understood but it's believed to be related to its inhibition of HER2 signalling, which also plays a role in the heart. It's important to monitor cardiac function before and during treatment with trastuzumab.
  • Infliximab and Adalimumab are TNF-alpha inhibitors used to treat autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease. Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody used to treat B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma and CLL. These drugs are not known to cause cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman goes to her dermatologist to have a mole removed. The patient tells her physician that she had an allergic reaction to a local anesthetic the last time she had dental work performed. Examination of her dental records by her dentist reveals that the patient received procaine for a tooth extraction. Which of the following drugs would be appropriate for the present procedure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Mepivacaine

 

The patient had a reaction to procaine, a type of ester local anaesthetic. An allergy to one type of ester local anaesthetic could potentially mean that she may react to other types of ester local anaesthetics, since they have similar structures and are metabolized in a similar way. Benzocaine, chloroprocaine and cocaine are all ester local anaesthetics, so should be avoided in this patient. It would be safest to use an amide local anaesthetic in this patient. The only amide anaesthetic in the choices is Mepivacaine.

questions.stem: Epinephrine added to a solution of lignocaine for a peripheral nerve block will:

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the duration of action of the local anesthetic

questions.answerText: Increase the duration of action of the local anesthetic
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Increase the duration of action of the local anesthetic

 

  • Epinephrine (also known as adrenaline) is often added to local anaesthetics to prolong their effect. It achieves this by causing vasoconstriction, which slows the absorption of the anaesthetic into the bloodstream. This allows the anaesthetic to stay in the injected area for a longer period of time, extending the duration of numbness.
  • Therefore, the answer would be B. Increase the duration of action of the local anaesthetic.
  • Epinephrine does not increase the risk of convulsions. In fact, it might reduce the risk, because by slowing the absorption of the anaesthetic into the bloodstream, it reduces the risk of toxic levels of the drug reaching the brain, which could potentially cause convulsions.

questions.stem: A drug that binds to and inhibits Gp IIb /IIIa glycoprotein and is responsible for platelet antiaggregatory effects is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Tirofiban

 

  • Tirofiban is a drug that specifically binds to and inhibits the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor on platelets. The glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor plays a crucial role in platelet aggregation, as it is involved in the final step of platelet aggregation by mediating the binding of fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor to platelets. By inhibiting this receptor, tirofiban prevents the cross-linking of platelets and inhibits platelet aggregation, leading to antiaggregatory effects.
  • Clopidogrel (Option A) is an antiplatelet drug that works by irreversible inhibition of the P2Y12 receptors of ADP on platelets.
  • Enoxaparin (Option B) is a low molecular weight heparin that primarily acts as an anticoagulant by activating anti-thrombin.
  • Fondaparinux (Option C) is also an anticoagulant that selectively inhibits factor Xa.

questions.stem: Postoperative vomiting is uncommon with this intravenous anaesthetic agent and patient are able to ambulate sooner than those who receive other anaesthetic agents?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Propofol

  • Propofol is an intravenous anaesthetic agent that is known for its favorable postoperative profile. It is associated with a lower incidence of postoperative vomiting compared to other anaesthetic agents. Postoperative vomiting can be a common side effect of anaesthesia, but propofol has been found to have antiemetic properties and is less likely to cause this adverse effect.
  • Additionally, patients who receive propofol as an anaesthetic agent are generally able to ambulate sooner compared to those who receive other agents. Propofol has a rapid onset and offset of action, allowing for a smooth recovery and faster awakening from anaesthesia. Its short duration of action enables patients to regain consciousness and mobility more quickly, facilitating early ambulation.
  • All of these features make propofol the drug of choice for day care surgery.
  • Regarding other options:
    • Ketamine (Option A) is a dissociative anaesthetic that is known to cause postoperative hallucinations and emergence reactions.
    • Enflurane (Option B) is an inhalation anaesthetic that is no longer commonly used due to its potential side effects.
    • Remifentanil (Option D) is an opioid analgesic that does not have direct effects on postoperative vomiting or ambulation.

questions.stem: Long term use of pethidine is avoided because a metabolite of pethidine is associated with:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Seizures

 

  • Long-term use of pethidine (also known as meperidine) is generally avoided due to the association of its metabolite, norpethidine, with seizures.
  • Norpethidine is a metabolite of pethidine that can accumulate in the body with prolonged use, leading to central nervous system stimulation and seizures.
  • This can be particularly concerning in patients with impaired kidney function, as norpethidine has a longer half-life in such individuals, increasing the risk of seizures.
  • Therefore, pethidine is typically reserved for short-term use or in specific situations where other opioid analgesics are contraindicated.


ore, pethidine is typically reserved for short-term use or in specific situations where other opioid analgesics are contraindicated.

questions.stem: A psychiatric patient taking medication develops a tremor, thyroid enlargement and leucocytosis. Drug implicated is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Lithium

  • The symptoms described, including tremor, thyroid enlargement (goiter), and leucocytosis, are associated with the use of lithium.
  • Tremor is a well-known side effect of lithium and can manifest as fine hand tremors even within therapeutic plasma concentration.
  • Thyroid enlargement or goiter can occur in some individuals taking lithium, and it may be associated with alterations in thyroid function. Leucocytosis, an increase in the white blood cell count, has also been reported as a potential side effect of lithium.
  • Important points regarding lithium can be remembered from this mnemonic:

LI: Leucocytes Increase

T: Tremors

H: Hypothyroidism

IU: Increased Urine

M: Mothers (avoided in pregnancy due to risk of Ebstein’s anomaly)

  • Regarding other options:
    • Clomipramine (Option A) is a tricyclic antidepressant commonly used in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
    • Haloperidol (Option B) is an antipsychotic medication, and while it can cause extrapyramidal symptoms like tremor, it does not typically cause thyroid enlargement or leucocytosis.
    • Olanzapine (Option D) is another antipsychotic medication that does not typically cause these specific side effects.

questions.stemHtml: Relative intensities of blocking effect (shown by symbol of +) of four drugs on different receptors is? Which drug is most likely to exacerbate the symptoms of Parkinsonism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Drug D

  • Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by a deficiency of dopamine, which leads to motor symptoms like bradykinesia, tremors, rigidity, and postural instability. The disease affects the dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of the brain, which normally send signals to the striatum to regulate movements. With the loss of these neurons, the balance between the excitatory (cholinergic) and inhibitory (dopaminergic) signals is disrupted, leading to the motor symptoms.
  • Drugs with high D2 receptor blocking effects would potentially exacerbate the symptoms of Parkinsonism as they would further decrease dopamine activity. Hence, looking at the table, Drug A and Drug D have significant D2 receptor blocking effects (+++). However, Drug A also has muscarinic receptor blocking effects which might reduce the symptoms of Parkinson's (as muscarinic blocking can reduce the overactivity of the cholinergic system).
  • Considering all these factors, the most likely drug to exacerbate the symptoms of Parkinsonism among the options provided would be Drug D.

questions.stem: High cumulative doses of Bleomycin are associated with:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Pulmonary fibrosis

 

  • High cumulative doses of Bleomycin are associated with pulmonary fibrosis.
  • Pulmonary fibrosis is a serious side effect of Bleomycin therapy and can lead to progressive scarring and damage to lung tissue.
  • It is characterized by the formation of excessive fibrous tissue in the lungs, impairing their normal function. Pulmonary fibrosis can cause shortness of breath, cough, and reduced lung capacity.
  • Regular monitoring of lung function is important during Bleomycin treatment to detect and manage any potential pulmonary complications.
  • Cardiotoxicity is major adverse effect of anthracyclines like doxorubicin and daunorubicin. This adverse effect can be prevented by dexrazoxane.
  • Hemorrhagic cystitis is an adverse effect of cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide. It can be prevented by pre-treatment with mesna.
  • Peripheral neuropathy is caused by vinca alkaloids like vincristine and vinblastine.

questions.stem: The drug reducing need of platelet transfusion in patients undergoing cancer chemotherapy is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Oprelvekin

 

  • Oprelvekin, also known as interleukin-11 (IL-11), is a medication that stimulates the production of platelets in the body. It works by binding to specific receptors on cells in the bone marrow, stimulating the production of megakaryocytes, which are the precursors to platelets. This leads to increased platelet production and helps to prevent or reduce the need for platelet transfusions in patients undergoing chemotherapy, particularly those with solid tumors or non-myeloid malignancies.
  • Regarding other options
    • Erythropoietin is a medication that stimulates the production of red blood cells. It is primarily used to treat anaemia, particularly in patients with chronic kidney disease or those undergoing certain cancer treatments. 
    • Filgrastim is a medication that stimulates the production of white blood cells, specifically neutrophils. It is commonly used to reduce the risk of infection in patients undergoing chemotherapy or bone marrow transplantation. 
    • Sargramostim, also known as granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), is a medication that stimulates the production of various white blood cells, including granulocytes and macrophages. Similar to filgrastim, it is primarily used to boost the immune system and reduce the risk of infection in patients undergoing certain cancer treatments or bone marrow transplantation.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician for a severe sore throat. The pediatrician prescribes penicillin and sends the girl home. Later that day, she develops a diffuse maculopapular rash, shortness of breath, and wheezing. Her parents take her to the emergency department, where she is diagnosed with anaphylaxis and treated successfully with epinephrine. Three months later, the girl has dysuria and urinary frequency. Urine Gram's stain reveals numerous gram-negative rods. Which of the following antibiotics could be safely given to this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Aztreonam

 

  • Aztreonam is a monobactam that is structurally different from penicillin and does not cross-react with penicillin allergies. It is effective against many gram-negative bacteria and can be used as an alternative in patients with a documented penicillin allergy.
  • The other antibiotic options listed are:
    • Ampicillin is a penicillin and should be avoided in patients with a documented penicillin allergy due to the risk of cross-reactivity.
    • Cefoperazone is a cephalosporin, which also has a risk of cross-reactivity with penicillin allergies. It should be avoided in patients with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin.
    • Cephalexin is another cephalosporin and can also cross-react with penicillin allergies. It should be avoided in patients with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin.

questions.stem: A worried mother complains to her pediatrician that both she and her 8-year-old son's teacher have noticed that the child has become inattentive. She states that her son frequently stops what he is doing and "stares blankly into space" before resuming his activities. Electroencephalography reveals a 3/second spike and slow wave pattern of discharges. Which of the following agents would most effectively treat this child's disorder?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Valproate

 

  • Based on the description of the child's symptoms and the electroencephalography findings, it appears that the child is experiencing absence seizures, also known as petit mal epilepsy. Absence seizures are characterized by brief lapses of consciousness, during which the person appears to be staring blankly into space.
  • Drug of choice for treatment of absence seizures is valproate. Another first line drug for treating absence seizures is Ethosuximide.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with severe bronchial asthma presents with white patches on the inside of the cheeks that can be easily wiped off, leaving a red, bleeding, sore surface. He is currently using beclomethasone and formoterol inhalers for his asthma and he is allergic to penicillin. Which of the following agents would be most appropriate for the treatment of this patient's oral condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Nystatin

 

  • The description of white patches on the inside of the cheeks that can be easily wiped off, leaving a red, bleeding, sore surface suggests the presence of oral thrush, which is a fungal infection caused by Candida species.
  • Nystatin is an antifungal medication commonly used to treat oral thrush. It is effective against Candida species and is available as an oral suspension or lozenges. Nystatin is a polyene drug similar to amphotericin B and works by binding to the fungal cell membrane, causing leakage of intracellular contents and ultimately leading to the death of the fungus.
  • Acyclovir (option A) is an antiviral medication whereas Amoxicillin (option B) and Cefixime (option C) are both anti-bacterials. They would not be effective against a fungal infection like oral thrush.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with well-controlled Parkinson's disease and type 2 diabetes presents with akinesia, a festinating gait, rigidity, and loss of postural reflexes. The patient states that his symptoms began shortly after starting a new "stomach" medication. On the basis of this information, the patient is most likely receiving?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Metoclopramide

 

  • Based on the patient's symptoms and the timing of their onset after starting a new medication, the most likely medication the patient is receiving that could be causing these symptoms is metoclopramide (option B).
  • Metoclopramide is a medication commonly used to treat gastrointestinal disorders such as gastroparesis, acid reflux, and vomiting. However, it is known to have central nervous system effects, particularly on the dopamine receptors. It can block dopamine receptors in the brain, leading to extrapyramidal symptoms similar to those seen in Parkinson's disease. These symptoms include akinesia (loss of voluntary movement), a festinating gait (small, shuffling steps), rigidity, and loss of postural reflexes.
  • Cisapride (option A) is another gastrointestinal medication used to treat conditions such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and gastroparesis, but it does not block D2 receptors in the central nervous system.
  • Nizatidine (option C) and omeprazole (option D) are medications used to reduce stomach acid production and treat conditions such as peptic ulcers and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). They do not typically cause the extrapyramidal symptoms described in the patient.

questions.stem: While rescuing a child from a burning home, a firefighter was burned over 60% of his body. He is rushed to the emergency room and quickly taken into surgery. During the surgery, the anesthesiologist notices tall, peaked T waves and prolongation of the PR interval, accompanied by progressive widening of the QRS complex so that it appears to merge with the T waves. The patient goes into ventricular fibrillation, then asystole, and cannot be resuscitated. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible for this patient's electrocardiographic changes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Succinylcholine

  • The electrocardiographic changes described in the scenario, including tall, peaked T waves, prolongation of the PR interval, progressive widening of the QRS complex, and subsequent ventricular fibrillation and asystole, are indicative of hyperkalemia.
  • Among the options provided, the agent most likely responsible for the patient's electrocardiographic changes and subsequent cardiac arrest is Succinylcholine (option D).
  • Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent commonly used in anaesthesia for rapid sequence induction and tracheal intubation. However, it is known to cause a transient increase in serum potassium levels, especially in patients with burns or crush injuries. This increase in potassium can lead to hyperkalemia, which can affect the electrical conduction of the heart and cause the observed ECG changes and cardiac arrest.
  • Atracurium (option A) and other non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents do not typically cause hyperkalemia.
  • Baclofen (option B) is a muscle relaxant used in the treatment of spasticity. It does not typically cause hyperkalemia or the described ECG changes.

Halothane (option C) is an inhalation anaesthetic. While it can cause hepatotoxicity and malignant hyperthermia, it is not directly associated with hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old female patient presents with complaints of a non-productive cough, low-grade fever, and a headache. The physician also notes a non-purulent otitis media. She is treated with an antibiotic that inhibits the translocation of the growing peptide chain along the mRNA. The antibiotic the patient was given was?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Erythromycin
  • Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that acts by binding to the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome and inhibiting the translocation step of protein synthesis. By interfering with translocation, erythromycin prevents the elongation of the growing peptide chain, ultimately inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis.
  • Drugs inhibiting translocation are:
    • M:          Macrolides
    • C:           Clindamycin
    • Q:           Quinpristin-dalfopristin
  • Chloramphenicol (option A) inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 50S subunit and preventing the formation of peptide bonds.
  • Amikacin (option B) is an aminoglycoside antibiotic that acts by binding to the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome and interfering with the initiation complex.
  • Doxycycline (option D) is a tetracycline antibiotic that acts by binding to the 30S subunit and inhibiting the binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the mRNA-ribosome complex.

questions.stem: Metronidazole is least likely to be effective in treatment of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Pneumocytosis

 

  • Metronidazole is an antibiotic that is effective against anaerobic bacteria and some protozoal infections.
  • It is commonly used to treat infections caused by Bacteroides fragilis, including intra-abdominal infections, hepatic amebiasis, and certain types of colitis such as pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridium difficile.
  • However, metronidazole is not effective against Pneumocystis jirovecii, the causative agent of pneumocystosis (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia or PCP).
  • Drug of choice for treatment of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is cotrimoxazole which is a combination of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).
  • Uses of metronidazole include:
    • G:   Giardiasis
              Gardnerella vaginalis (Bacterial vaginosis)
    • U:   Ulcer (Peptic ulcer associated with H pylori)
    • P:   Pseudomembranous colitis
    • T:   Trichomoniasis
    • A:   Anaerobic bacterial infections (e.g. Bacterides fragilis)
              Amoebiasis

questions.stem: True statement regarding vancomycin is:

options.label: B
options.text: It has the advantage of oral bioavailability

options.label: C
options.text: It is not susceptible to penicillinases

options.label: D
options.text: Staphylococcal enterocolits occurs commonly with its use

questions.answerText: It is not susceptible to penicillinases
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. It is not susceptible to penicillinases

 

  • Vancomycin is a bactericidal antibiotic that inhibits cell wall synthesis in bacteria. Unlike penicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics, vancomycin is not susceptible to the action of penicillinases, which are enzymes produced by some bacteria that can inactivate penicillins. This makes vancomycin an effective alternative for treating infections caused by bacteria that produce penicillinases, such as certain strains of Staphylococcus aureus.

 

The other statements provided are false:

 

  1. Vancomycin is bactericidal, not bacteriostatic. It kills bacteria rather than just inhibiting their growth.
  2. Vancomycin has poor oral bioavailability and is typically administered intravenously. Oral vancomycin is primarily used to treat infections in the gastrointestinal tract, such as Clostridium difficile-associated colitis, but its systemic bioavailability is low.
  3. Staphylococcal enterocolitis is not a common side effect associated with vancomycin use. While vancomycin can disrupt the normal microbial flora of the gut and potentially lead to antibiotic-associated diarrhea or colitis, this is more commonly associated with the overgrowth of Clostridium difficile, rather than Staphylococcus species.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibiotics is NOT effective against pseudomonas infections?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Vancomycin

  • Among the antibiotics mentioned, Vancomycin is not effective against Pseudomonas infections.
  • Vancomycin is primarily used to treat Gram-positive bacterial infections, such as those caused by
    • Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant strains) and Enterococcus species.
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is a common pathogen associated with Pseudomonas infections, is inherently resistant to Vancomycin.
  • The other antibiotics mentioned—Ceftazidime, Ciprofloxacin, and Rifampicin—are known to have activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and can be used to treat infections caused by this bacterium.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the clinic with a palpable lump in her left breast that she noticed while showering. She reports no associated pain, discharge, or skin changes. Her past medical history is unremarkable and she has no known family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Her last mammogram was two years ago and showed no abnormalities. After appropriate investigations including mammogram, ultrasound, and biopsy, she is diagnosed with stage II breast cancer. The biopsy reveals that the cancer is HER2-positive, but estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) negative. Which of the following drugs, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, would be suitable for treating this patient's breast cancer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Lapatinib

  • Lapatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that is commonly used in the treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer. In this case, the patient has been diagnosed with stage II breast cancer that is HER2-positive but estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) negative. Lapatinib is effective in targeting the HER2 receptor, which is overexpressed in HER2-positive breast cancer cells. Other tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for breast cancer is neratinib.
  • Sorafenib (Option A) is primarily used in the treatment of renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • Imatinib (Option B) is drug of choice for the treatment of CML and GIST.
  • Pazopanib (Option C) is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in the treatment of advanced renal cell carcinoma and soft tissue sarcoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding sedative hypnotic drugs is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Benzodiazepines exhibit a steeper dose response relationship as compared to barbiturates

options.label: B
options.text: Barbiturates may increase the half-lives of drugs metabolized by the liver

options.label: C
options.text: Alkalization of the urine will accelerate the elimination of phenobarbitone

options.label: D
options.text: Respiratory depression caused by barbiturate overdosage can be reversed by flumazenil

questions.answerText: Alkalization of the urine will accelerate the elimination of phenobarbitone
questions.solutionHtml:
f phenobarbitone

Explanation:

    • Benzodiazepines actually have a safer (flat) dose-response curve compared to barbiturates. Barbiturates have a steep dose-response curve, meaning a small increase in dose can lead to a large increase in drug effect, potentially leading to fatal overdose.
    • Barbiturates are known to induce liver enzymes, which can speed up the metabolism of other drugs. This effect can decrease the half-life of those drugs.
    • Alkalization of the urine can accelerate the elimination of phenobarbital. This drug is weakly acidic and its elimination can be enhanced in an alkaline environment.
    • Flumazenil is an antagonist of benzodiazepines, not barbiturates. It is used to reverse benzodiazepine overdoses and will not effectively reverse respiratory depression caused by barbiturate overdosage.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of epilepsy has been taking phenytoin for seizure control. After starting another drug, plasma concentration of phenytoin was found to be 25 mcg/ml (therapeutic levels are 10-20 mcg/ml). This sudden rise in plasma drug concentration of phenytoin can cause which of the following adverse effects?
questions.solutionHtml:
rong>

 

Explanation:

 

Phenytoin is known to have several potential side effects that can become more apparent or severe as the level of the drug in the bloodstream increases beyond therapeutic levels. This phenomenon is often described as "dose-dependent toxicity."

 

  1. Ataxia, or a lack of muscle control during voluntary movements, can occur as a side effect of high levels of phenytoin. This could result in unsteady movements and difficulty with coordination.
  2. Arrhythmias are also noted with high plasma levels of phenytoin.

 

Other adverse effects of phenytoin like hirsutism and gum hyperplasia are seen on long term use (chronic) only.

 

Adverse Effects of Phenytoin:

 

H:    Hirsutism

O:    Osteomalacia

T:    Teratogenicity (Fetal Hydantoin Syndrome)

M:   Megaloblastic anemia

A:    Arrhythmia (Acute side effect seen at overdose only)

L:     Lymphadenopathy

I:     Increase in blood glucose (due to inhibition of insulin release)

K:     Vitamin K deficiency

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs has a high affinity for 5-HT2 receptors in the brain, does not cause extrapyramidal dysfunction or agranulocytosis, and is reported to increase the risk of significant QT prolongation?
questions.solutionHtml:
or:black;font-size:12.0pt;">Ans. D. Ziprasidone

 

Explanation:

 

  • Ziprasidone is an atypical antipsychotic that acts by blocking dopamine (D2) and serotonin (5-HT2) receptors in the brain. It is known to have less risk of causing extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) or agranulocytosis compared to other antipsychotics. However, it has been associated with a risk of QT prolongation, a specific type of abnormal heart rhythm that can potentially lead to serious complications such as Torsades de pointes or sudden cardiac death.
  • Chlorpromazine is a typical antipsychotic that can cause extrapyramidal symptoms.
  • Clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic, has a risk of causing agranulocytosis (a severe and dangerous decrease in white blood cells), which necessitates routine blood monitoring.
  • Olanzapine is an atypical antipsychotic and while it does have a high affinity for 5-HT2 receptors and does not typically cause agranulocytosis, it is not specifically associated with a high risk of QT prolongation.

questions.stem: All of the following limitations of typical tricyclic antidepressants has been overcome by selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors except?

options.label: A
options.text: Frequent anticholinergic, sedative and hypotensive side effects

options.label: B
options.text: High risk of cardiac arrhythmias and seizures in overdose

questions.solutionHtml:
12.0pt;">Ans. C. Delayed response

 

Explanation:

 

  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) typically have fewer anticholinergic, sedative, and hypotensive side effects than tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs).
  • SSRIs have a safer profile in terms of overdose than TCAs. Overdose with TCAs can lead to severe cardiac arrhythmias and seizures, while overdose with SSRIs is generally much less dangerous.
  • Both SSRIs and TCAs typically take a few weeks to exert their full therapeutic effects. Thus, the delayed response is not a limitation that has been overcome by SSRIs.
  • SSRIs generally have less of an impact on metabolic parameters, including acid-base balance, than TCAs, so they're less likely to cause metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: Patients should be cautioned not to consume alcohol when given a prescription for any of the following except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Ofloxacin

 

  • All the drugs mentioned in the question ie chlorpropamide, griseofulvin and metronidazole are associated with disulfiram like reaction with alcohol intake. Fluoroquinolones like Ofloxacin are devoid of this adverse effect.
  • A disulfiram-like reaction refers to a syndrome that mimics the effects seen with the drug disulfiram, which is used in the treatment of chronic alcoholism. Disulfiram works by inhibiting an enzyme involved in metabolizing alcohol, specifically aldehyde dehydrogenase. This results in an accumulation of acetaldehyde, a toxic metabolite of alcohol, which causes unpleasant symptoms like flushing (sudden redness and warmth in the face), Tachycardia (rapid heart rate), Shortness of breath, Nausea and vomiting, Headache, Sweating, Hypotension (may cause dizziness or fainting), Confusion and blurred vision etc.
  • Drugs causing disulfiram like reaction include:
    • Cyclic: Chlorpropamide, Ceforperazone
    • G: Griseofulvin
    • M: Metronidazole
    • P: Procarbazine

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presents to his primary care physician complaining of a persistent, dull, gnawing pain in his upper abdomen. He mentions the discomfort has been on and off for several months now and seems to worsen on an empty stomach. He denies any changes in bowel habits or any symptoms of nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. His medical history is notable for osteoarthritis and he has been taking aspirin regularly for the past 5 years for pain relief. The physician suspects that chronic use of aspirin may have led to the development of a peptic ulcer. Which of the following drugs would be the best choice for treating this patient's suspected peptic ulcer disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
ns. A) Omeprazole

 

Explanation:

 

  • Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and is generally considered the first-line treatment for peptic ulcer disease, including ulcers that are suspected to have been caused by chronic NSAID (such as aspirin) use.
  • Omeprazole and other PPIs work by irreversibly inhibiting the hydrogen/potassium ATPase pump in the stomach lining, which is responsible for the final step in the production of gastric acid. This reduces the amount of acid in the stomach, allowing ulcers to heal and reducing the likelihood of their formation.
  • Misoprostol is a prostaglandin analog and is most specific drug for NSAID-induced ulcers. It acts by increasing bicarbonate and mucus production in the stomach, thereby protecting the stomach lining. However, it's often not the first choice due to its side effects (such as diarrhea) and the need for frequent dosing (four times daily).
  • Pirenzepine is a selective M1 muscarinic receptor antagonist that inhibits gastric acid secretion, but it is less effective and commonly used than PPIs or H2 blockers in peptic ulcer disease.
  • Ranitidine is a H2-receptor antagonist and while it also decreases the production of stomach acid, it is not as potent as PPIs like omeprazole.

questions.stem: A patient on cisplatin therapy develops intractable vomiting on the third day of treatment. Agent of choice for controlling this vomiting is:
questions.solutionHtml:
ong>Ans. A. Netupitant

 

Explanation:

 

  • Cisplatin is a chemotherapeutic agent that is associated with a high risk of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV). It can cause two types of vomiting.
    • Early vomiting: It occurs within first 24 hours of administration of cisplatin. 5-HT3 receptor antagonists like ondansetron are drug of choice for managing early CINV.
    • Delayed vomiting: It occurs after first day of administration of cisplatin. NK1 receptor anatagonists like aprepitant, netupitant etc are DOC for delayed CINV.
  • Netupitant is a NK1 receptor antagonist and is usually used in combination with a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist (like palonosetron) and dexamethasone. It is DOC for delayed CINV associated with highly emetogenic chemotherapy.
  • Ondansetron is often the first choice for managing acute CINV due to its efficacy and tolerability.
  • Metoclopramide, a dopamine receptor antagonist, may be used to manage CINV, but it's generally not as effective as the 5-HT3 antagonists.
  • Prochlorperazine is also used to manage CINV, but it's not generally the first choice because of its potential to cause extrapyramidal symptoms.

questions.stem: Choose the correct statement about the use of loperamide in the management of diarrhea:

options.label: A
options.text: It is used to control diarrhea irrespective of its etiology

options.label: B
options.text: It should be used only as a short term measure after ensuring that enteroinvasive organisms are not involved

options.label: C
options.text: It is used as adjuvant to antimicrobial therapy of diarrhea

options.label: D
options.text: It is the drug of choice in Traveller’s diarrhea

questions.answerText: It should be used only as a short term measure after ensuring that enteroinvasive organisms are not involved
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

  • Loperamide is an anti-diarrheal agent that works by slowing the movement of the intestines, which helps to reduce the frequency of bowel movements.
  • It is not used to control diarrhea irrespective of its etiology. For instance, if diarrhea is caused by certain types of infections (such as those involving enteroinvasive organisms), loperamide can potentially worsen the situation by delaying the elimination of the pathogens from the gut.
  • Loperamide is used as a short-term measure to manage symptoms of acute diarrhea. It is especially important to confirm that enteroinvasive organisms are not involved, as using loperamide in such cases could be harmful.
  • Loperamide is not used as an adjuvant to antimicrobial therapy. It is primarily used for symptomatic relief.
  • Loperamide is not the drug of choice for Traveller's diarrhea, especially when the diarrhea is severe, bloody, or accompanied by fever. Antibiotics are often the preferred treatment in such cases.


erred treatment in such cases.

questions.stem: Which of the following anti-tubercular drugs is safe in hepatitis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Streptomycin

 

Read the options carefully, option C is ethionamide and not ethambutol. Ethionamide is hepatotoxic whereas ethambutol is not.

 

  • Antitubercular drugs which are not hepatotoxic include ethambutol and streptomycin
  • Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used in the treatment of tuberculosis, particularly in cases of drug-resistant TB or when other first-line drugs cannot be used due to contraindications or intolerance. It is usually safe to use in patients with hepatitis, as it is primarily excreted by the kidneys and does not have significant hepatotoxicity.
  • Isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide are first-line anti-tubercular drugs whereas ethionamide is second line antitubercular drug which are hepatotoxic.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a myocardial infarction. Angioplasty and stenting are not possible because the cardiac cath lab is busy with other high-priority patients, so administration of a thrombolytic drug is the only option. Which one of the following is the most important determinant, overall, of the success of thrombolytic therapy in terms of salvaging viable cardiac muscle?

options.label: A
options.text: Choosing a “human” t-PA like alteplase, rather than one that is bacterial-derived like streptokinase

options.label: B
options.text: Infarct location (i.e., anterior wall of left ventricular vs. another site/wall)

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of collateral blood vessels to the infarct-related coronary artery

options.label: D
options.text: Time from onset of infarction to administration of the thrombolytic agent

questions.answerText: Time from onset of infarction to administration of the thrombolytic agent
questions.solutionHtml:
ime from onset of infarction to administration of the thrombolytic agent

Explanation:

  • The benefit of thrombolytic therapy in myocardial infarction is highly dependent on the time from onset of symptoms to administration of the thrombolytic agent. The earlier the treatment is initiated, the more heart muscle can be saved, reducing the extent of damage and improving the prognosis. This principle is often referred to as "time is muscle" in cardiology.
  • The choice between different types of thrombolytic agents (like alteplase, a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator, versus streptokinase, a bacterial-derived drug) can be important, but the most critical factor is generally the speed of administration.
  • While the location of the infarct can affect the prognosis (anterior wall infarcts are typically more serious), it does not determine the success of thrombolytic therapy per se.
  • The presence of collateral blood vessels may help preserve heart tissue during an infarct, but again, this does not determine the success of thrombolytic therapy itself.
  • Overall, the most important determinant of the success of thrombolytic therapy in terms of salvaging viable cardiac muscle is the time from onset of infarction to administration of the thrombolytic agent.


erred to as "time is muscle" in cardiology.

questions.stem: The combination of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole is effective against which of the following opportunistic infections in the AIDS patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
cystis jiroveci

 

Explanation:

 

  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), also known as co-trimoxazole, is a combination antibiotic that is effective against a wide range of bacteria. It is also the treatment and prophylaxis of choice for Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii) pneumonia, an opportunistic infection that is common in individuals with AIDS.
  • Disseminated Herpes simplex is generally treated with antiviral drugs, such as acyclovir.
  • Cryptococcal meningitis is typically treated with a combination of antifungal medications, often including amphotericin B and flucytosine.
  • Tuberculosis is typically treated with a combination of anti-tubercular drugs, such as isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide.

questions.stem: Which of the following is used for the radical cure of Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Artemisinin based combination therapy

Read the question carefully. The question is asked about radical cure of P. falciparum malaria. As P. falciparum does not have hypnozoite state (no relapse), so the clinical cure itself can be considered as radical cure. Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is currently the most effective treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

  • It should be noted that while Primaquine (option c) is not primarily used for treating Plasmodium falciparum, it is used for a "radical cure" of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale to eradicate the dormant liver stages and prevent relapse. Primaquine can be used as gameticidal drug for P falciparum malaria.
  • Chloroquine (option a) is drug of choice for P. vivax malaria resistance of Plasmodium falciparum to this drug has become widespread in many areas and it is thus not preferred for P falciparum malaria.
  • Doxycycline (option d) is an antibiotic that can be used in combination with other drugs for malaria prophylaxis and treatment, but it is not the frontline therapy for Plasmodium falciparum malaria.


ully. The question is asked about radical cure of P. falciparum malaria. As P. falciparum does not have hypnozoite state (no relapse), so the clinical cure itself can be considered as radical cure. Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is currently the most effective treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

options.label: C

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the fluoroquinolones is FALSE?

options.label: A
options.text: Gonococcal resistance to fluoroquinolones may involve changes in DNA gyrase

options.label: B
options.text: Modification of ciprofloxacin dosage is required in patients if creatinine clearance is less than 50 mL/min

options.label: C
options.text: Norfloxacin is the drug of choice for treatment of an uncomplicated urinary tract infection in a 7 year-old girl

options.label: D
options.text: Fluoroquinolones inhibit relaxation of positively supercoiled DNA

questions.answerText: Norfloxacin is the drug of choice for treatment of an uncomplicated urinary tract infection in a 7 year-old girl
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Norfloxacin is the drug of choice for treatment of an uncomplicated urinary tract infection in a 7 year-old girl

  • Fluoroquinolones, including norfloxacin, are generally not recommended for use in children due to the risk of developing musculoskeletal disorders such as tendonitis and tendon rupture. Other classes of antibiotics, such as cephalosporins, penicillins, and nitrofurantoin, are usually preferred for treating uncomplicated urinary tract infections in children.
  • Fluoroquinolones work by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, which are enzymes that manage the supercoiling of DNA. When these enzymes are inhibited, the DNA becomes overwound or "positively supercoiled," which disrupts essential DNA processes and ultimately leads to bacterial death. So, fluoroquinolones inhibit the relaxation of positively supercoiled DNA.
  • Fluoroquinolones work by inhibiting bacterial enzymes like DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, which
    • are essential for bacterial DNA replication. Resistance to fluoroquinolones often involves changes (mutations) in these target enzymes, including DNA gyrase. In Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, such changes contribute to fluoroquinolone resistance.
  • Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that is excreted primarily through the kidneys. If a patient has impaired kidney function, as indicated by a creatinine clearance of less than 50 mL/min, they may not be able to eliminate the drug as efficiently. As a result, dosage adjustments are often needed to avoid potential toxicity. Fluoroquinolones which do not require dose adjustment in renal failure are:
    • P:         Pefloxacin
    • M:        Moxifloxacin
    • T:         Trovafloxacin


erred for treating uncomplicated urinary tract infections in children.

questions.stem: A post operative patient developed septicemia and was empirically started on combination chemotherapy by a new resident doctor. However, when the patient did not respond even after 10 days of antibiotics treatment, the review of the charts was done. It was found that that the resident doctor had started the combination of antibiotics which was mutually antagonistic in action. Which of the following is the most likely combination that was given?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Ampicillin and Chloramphenicol

 

  • Ampicillin is a bactericidal antibiotic that works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis. On the other hand, Chloramphenicol is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that works by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. When used together, the bacteriostatic action of Chloramphenicol can interfere with the bactericidal action of Ampicillin. This phenomenon, where one antibiotic interferes with the effectiveness of another, is known as antibiotic antagonism.
  • As for the other options:
    • Vancomycin and Amikacin (A) are both bactericidal and are often used together in serious infections without antagonism.
    • Cephalexin and Gentamicin (C) also act in a synergistic way against many types of bacteria and are not antagonistic.
    • Ciprofloxacin and Piperacillin (D) also have different mechanisms of action but are not known to be antagonistic when used together.

questions.stem: Regarding the antibacterial action of amikacin, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Antibacterial activity is often reduced by the presence of an inhibitor of cell wall synthesis

options.label: B
options.text: It continues to exert antibacterial effects even after plasma levels decrease below detectable range

options.label: C
options.text: Efficacy is directly proportionate to the time that the plasma level of the drug is greater than the minimal inhibitory concentration

options.label: D
options.text: It has strong antibacterial activity against Salmonella

questions.answerText: It continues to exert antibacterial effects even after plasma levels decrease below detectable range
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. It continues to exert antibacterial effects even after plasma levels decrease below detectable range

  • Amikacin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic. Aminoglycosides, including amikacin, are known to exhibit "post-antibiotic effect" (PAE). The PAE is a period of continued bacterial growth suppression that persists after the antibiotic concentration has fallen below the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of the bacteria.
  • To briefly touch on the other options:
    • Option a. Antibacterial activity is often reduced by the presence of an inhibitor of cell wall synthesis: This is generally not true. Aminoglycosides like amikacin actually have synergistic effects with beta-lactam antibiotics, which inhibit cell wall synthesis.
    • Option c. Efficacy is directly proportionate to the time that the plasma level of the drug is greater than the minimal inhibitory concentration: This is generally more applicable to drugs following time-dependent killing like beta lactams and vancomycin. Aminoglycosides like amikacin follow concentration-dependent killing, meaning their efficacy is more related to peak concentrations, rather than the duration that levels exceed the MIC.
    • Option d. It has strong antibacterial activity against Salmonella: Amikacin is typically more active against organisms like Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacteriaceae. Salmonella are generally resistant to aminoglycosides.

questions.stem: Which of the following combination of drug and its indication is FALSE?

options.label: C
options.text: Tafenoquine: Single dose treatment of P. falciparum malaria

options.label: D
options.text: Remdesivir: Moderate to severe COVID-19 pneumonia

questions.answerText: Tafenoquine: Single dose treatment of P. falciparum malaria
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Tafenoquine: Single dose treatment of P. falciparum malaria

  • Tafenoquine is an antimalarial medication, but it is used for the radical cure (prevention of relapse) of Plasmodium vivax malaria, not P. falciparum malaria.
  • As for the other options:
    • Pretomanid is used as part of a combination therapy for the treatment of multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB).
    • Fostemsavir is used for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in heavily treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection failing their current antiretroviral regimen.
    • Remdesivir is an antiviral medication that has been used for the treatment of COVID-19, including moderate to severe disease, particularly in hospitalized patients.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is the oral drug for treatment of mucormycosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Posaconazole

 

  • Posaconazole is an oral antifungal agent that can be used for the treatment of mucormycosis, also known as zygomycosis.
  • Amphotericin B (option A) is typically the first-line treatment for mucormycosis, but it is not available in an oral formulation; it is usually administered intravenously.
  • Voriconazole (option B) is drug of choice for aspergillosis, but it is not effective against Mucorales, the fungi that cause mucormycosis.
  • Terbinafine (option D) is an antifungal medication used mainly to treat fungal infections of the skin and nails, and is not used for mucormycosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about warfarin group of oral anticoagulatns is FALSE?

options.label: A
options.text: They interfere with an early step in the synthesis of clotting factors

options.label: B
options.text: Irrespective of the dose administered, their anticoagulant effect has a latency of onset of 4-5 days

options.label: C
options.text: Their dose is adjusted by repeated measurement of INR

options.label: D
options.text: It is contraindicated during first trimester of pregnancy

questions.answerText: They interfere with an early step in the synthesis of clotting factors
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. They interfere with an early step in the synthesis of clotting factors

  • Warfarin interferes with the recycling of vitamin K, which is necessary for the post-translational modification (carboxylation) of several clotting factors (II, VII, IX, and X). This modification is required for activation of these factors. Thus warfarin act by inhibiting the activation of clotting factors and not their synthesis.
  • The other options are all true:
  • Option b. Irrespective of the dose administered, their anticoagulant effect has a latency of onset of 4-5 days: It takes several days for warfarin to exert its full anticoagulant effect because it acts by inhibiting the activation of new clotting factors, not by deactivating existing clotting factors.
  • Option c. Their dose is adjusted by repeated measurement of INR: INR (International Normalized Ratio) is a laboratory measurement used to monitor the effects of warfarin and similar anticoagulants, and is used to adjust the drug dosage as necessary.
  • Option d. It is contraindicated during the first trimester of pregnancy: Warfarin is known to cross the placenta and can cause birth defects, especially when used during the first trimester.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had a heart transplant. She receives cyclosporine as part of the immunosuppressant regimen. Which of the following is the main mechanism of cyclosporine’s immunosuppressant effects?

options.label: A
options.text: Blocks the CD3 site on T lymphocytes, blocks all T cell functions

options.label: C
options.text: Directly inhibits B and T lymphocyte proliferation

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibits calcineurin and resulting IL-2 synthesis that is necessary for B and T cell proliferation

questions.answerText: Inhibits calcineurin and resulting IL-2 synthesis that is necessary for B and T cell proliferation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Inhibits calcineurin and resulting IL-2 synthesis that is necessary for B and T cell proliferation

 

Cyclosporine is an immunosuppressant that specifically inhibits the activity of calcineurin, a protein phosphatase involved in the activation of T cells. By inhibiting calcineurin, cyclosporine prevents the transcription of interleukin-2 (IL-2), a cytokine that is critical for the proliferation and activation of T cells. This mechanism makes cyclosporine effective in preventing organ transplant rejection.

questions.stem: A 67 years old female was given rivaroxaban to prevent thromboembolism after total knee replacement surgery. She took overdose of the above drug. Which of the following drug can be used to reverse the effect of the anticoagulant taken by her?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Andexanet alpha

 

  • Andexanet alpha is a recombinant modified human factor Xa decoy protein that is used as an antidote for the reversal of anticoagulation by Xa inhibitors like rivaroxaban.
  • Idarucizumab (option A) is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds to dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and reverses its anticoagulant effect.
  • Vitamin K (option B) is used to reverse the effects of vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants such as warfarin.
  • Protamine sulfate (option C) is used to reverse the effects of heparin.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about heparin is true?

options.label: A
options.text: It act by inhibiting anti-thrombin III

options.label: B
options.text: Heparin is preferred over warfarin for long-term treatment of DVT

options.label: C
options.text: Heparin has fewer drug interactions as compared to warfarin because it is metabolized by non-microsomal enzymes

questions.answerText: Heparin has fewer drug interactions as compared to warfarin because it is metabolized by non-microsomal enzymes
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Heparin has fewer drug interactions as compared to warfarin because it is metabolized by non-microsomal enzymes

 

  • Heparin acts as an anticoagulant by binding to antithrombin III and increasing its ability to inhibit thrombin and other proteases involved in blood clotting. It acts by activating anti-thrombin III and does not inhibit it, so option (A) is incorrect.
  • Heparin is often used for the initial, acute treatment of conditions like deep vein thrombosis (DVT), but for long-term treatment, warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are typically preferred due to their oral administration and other considerations. So, option (B) is also incorrect.
  • Heparin does generally have fewer drug interactions than warfarin, in part because it is not metabolized by the cytochrome P450 system, which is involved in the metabolism of many drugs. This makes option (C) correct.
  • Option (D) cannot be correct because both options (A) and (B) are incorrect.

questions.stem: Aducanumab is a recently approved new monoclonal antibody. It has been approved for treatment of?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Alzheimer's disease

  • Aducanumab is a monoclonal antibody that has been approved by the U.S. FDA for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. It works by targeting amyloid-beta plaques in the brain, which are a characteristic feature of Alzheimer's disease.
  • The other options:
    • Option b. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria: This is a rare blood disease treated with medications like eculizumab and ravulizumab, not aducanumab.
    • Option c. Non-small cell lung carcinoma: There are several monoclonal antibodies used in the treatment of non-small cell lung carcinoma, such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab, but aducanumab is not among them.
    • COVID-19: While monoclonal antibodies (like bamlanivimab and casirivimab/imdevimab) have been used in the treatment of COVID-19, aducanumab is not used for this purpose.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true of local anaesthetics?

options.label: A
options.text: The local anaesthetic is required in the unionized form for penetrating the neuronal membrane

options.label: B
options.text: The local anaesthetic approaches its receptor from the intraneuronal face of the Na+ channel

options.label: C
options.text: The local anaesthetic binds to its receptor mainly when the Na+ channel is in the resting state

options.label: D
options.text: The local anaesthetic combines with its receptor in the ionized cationic form

questions.answerText: The local anaesthetic binds to its receptor mainly when the Na+ channel is in the resting state
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. The local anaesthetic binds to its receptor mainly when the Na+ channel is in the resting state

  • Local anaesthetics primarily bind to their receptor, the voltage-gated sodium channel, when it's in the activated (open) or inactivated state, not the resting state. This is how they block sodium influx into the neuron, inhibiting the propagation of the action potential and resulting in a loss of sensation in the area where the anaesthetic is applied.
  • Regarding the other options:
    • The local anaesthetic is required in the unionized form for penetrating the neuronal membrane: This is true. Local anaesthetics exist in both ionized and unionized forms, and the unionized form is more lipophilic, allowing it to cross the cell membrane.
    • The local anaesthetic approaches its receptor from the intraneuronal face of the Na+ channel: This is also true. Once the local anaesthetic has crossed the cell membrane in its unionized form, it can ionize and bind to the sodium channel from the intracellular side.
    • The local anaesthetic combines with its receptor in the ionized cationic form: This is true as well. After the unionized form of the local anaesthetic penetrates the neuronal membrane, it can become ionized within the more acidic intracellular environment and bind to the sodium channel in its ionized form.

questions.stem: Mechanism of action of theophylline in bronchial asthma include all of the following except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Beta -2 receptor stimulation

 

  • Theophylline is a bronchodilator drug used in the treatment of asthma and other respiratory diseases, and it has multiple mechanisms of action:
    • Phosphodiesterase inhibition: This is one of the primary mechanisms of theophylline. By inhibiting phosphodiesterase enzymes, theophylline increases the level of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) in the cells, leading to smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation.
    • Adenosine receptor antagonism: Theophylline can also antagonize adenosine receptors, which can have a bronchodilator effect as well because adenosine can cause bronchoconstriction.
    • Increased histone deacetylation: This is a less well-understood mechanism of theophylline, but it's believed to have an anti-inflammatory effect in the lungs.
  • However, Theophylline does not directly stimulate beta-2 receptors, which is a mechanism of action of beta-2 agonists like salbutamol and salmeterol, not theophylline.

questions.stem: Which of the mechanism of antifungal drug is wrongly matched?

options.label: D
options.text: Amphotericin B- Create artificial pores in the membrane

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Flucytosine- Inhibit microtubule

  • Flucytosine does not inhibit microtubule formation. Instead, it works by penetrating fungal cells and being converted into 5-fluorouracil, which then inhibits thymidylate synthetase, an enzyme involved in DNA synthesis. This disrupts the synthesis of fungal DNA and proteins.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old male patient is currently receiving treatment in the oncology department for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). His oncologist has been discussing various therapeutic options with him, including a group of medications called immune checkpoint inhibitors. Immune checkpoints are regulators of the immune system that help to prevent the immune system from attacking cells indiscriminately. They do this by distinguishing between 'self' and 'non-self' cells. Some cancer cells can take advantage of these checkpoints to avoid being targeted by the immune system. Immune checkpoint inhibitors are a type of drug that blocks these immune checkpoints, allowing immune cells to better recognize and attack cancer cells. Given this information, which of the following drugs is not an immune check point inhibitor?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Cetuximab

 

  • Cetuximab is a monoclonal antibody, but it's not an immune checkpoint inhibitor. It is an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitor used for the treatment of colorectal cancer and non-small cell lung cancer. By binding to EGFR, cetuximab inhibits the activation and subsequent proliferation of the cancer cells.
  • On the other hand, Avelumab, Atezolizumab, and Durvalumab are all immune checkpoint inhibitors. They work by inhibiting the programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) on cancer cells, which prevents the cancer cells from using PD-L1 to "turn off" the immune system's T cells, thereby allowing the T cells to target the cancer cells.

 

Immune Check Point Inhibitors

questions.stem: Which of the following chelating agents can be used orally for the treatment of transfusion siderosis in thalassemia patients?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Deferipirone

  • Ferrioxamine is an iron containing compound. When we remove iron from this, the compound formed is called Desferrioxamine which has high affinity for iron.
  • Desferrioxamine (option A) is a chelating agent, but it is administered intravenously or through subcutaneous infusion. Desferrioxamine is commonly used for iron chelation therapy in thalassemia patients, but it is not administered orally.

questions.stem: Following the treatment of an oral abscess with clindamycin, a patient develops a greenish, foul-smelling watery diarrhea with left lower quadrant pain. Other signs and symptoms include fever, leukocytosis, and lethargy. If the toxin produced by Clostridium difficile is detected in the stool, the patient would most appropriately be treated with?

Ans. A. Fidaxomicin

  • Based on the scenario provided, the patient likely has pseudomembranous colitis, a common side effect of antibiotic treatment, particularly with broad-spectrum antibiotics like clindamycin. The symptoms described in the question: greenish, foul-smelling watery diarrhea, left lower quadrant pain, fever, leukocytosis, and lethargy – are consistent with this diagnosis and presence of toxin of Clostridium difficile in the stool confirms the diagnosis of pseudomembranous colitis.
  • Pseudomembranous colitis, also known as Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) is a common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and one of the primary treatments for CDI is antibiotics that specifically target the infection. Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic that is effective against Clostridium difficile and is now the drug of choice for treatment of pseudomembranous colitis.
  • The other options listed are:
  • Vancomycin is another antibiotic that is commonly used to treat CDI. However, vancomycin is no longer drug of choice for pseudomembranous colitis. Further, whenever used, vancomycin is preferred by oral route for treatment of this condition than by intravenous route.
  • Loperamide is an antidiarrheal medication that helps to relieve diarrhea symptoms by slowing down the movement of the intestines. However, it does not treat the underlying infection and would not be appropriate as the sole treatment for this patient.
  • Metronidazole is an antibiotic that has been used in the past as a first-line treatment for CDI. However, due to increasing resistance rates, current guidelines recommend reserving metronidazole for mild cases or as an alternative treatment option.
